'''John Fredrich Asmus''' (January 20, 1937 – March 31, 2024)<ref name="San Diego obit"/> was a research [[physicist]] who focused his work on the use of scientific techniques in [[art conservation]]. {{As of|2020}}, he taught at the Institute for Pure and Applied Physical Science at the [[University of California, San Diego]], where he began working in 1974.<ref>{{cite web|title=People - John Asmus - Brief Bio|url=http://can.ucsd.edu/people.php?selection=asmus|publisher=UC San Diego - Center for Advanced Nanoscience|language=en}}</ref>

Asmus was widely published, with over 125 articles published in professional journals and 25 patents to his name. Having received his PhD from the [[California Institute of Technology]], he initially applied his knowledge of high-energy [[excimer laser]]s in private sector organizations such as [[General Atomics]], where he contributed to the [[Project Orion (nuclear propulsion)|ORION]] nuclear spaceship program. Asmus then pioneered the use of [[holography]], lasers, [[ultrasonic imaging]], [[digital image processing]], and [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] in art conservation, working to preserve or investigate works as diverse as the statues in [[Venice]], frescoes of the [[California State Capitol]], petroglyphs in Utah's [[Arches National Park]], portraits by [[Rembrandt]], the [[Terracotta Army]] in [[Xi'an]], China, and the ''[[Mona Lisa]]''.

==Early life, education, and career==
Born in [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]], to William F. and Eleanor Emma (Kocher) Asmus, the family moved to [[San Diego, California]], in 1940. In the early 1950s, they moved to [[Montclair, California]], where Asmus attended [[Chaffey High School]].<ref name="San Diego obit"/>

Asmus worked for [[General Atomic]] in La Jolla, until 1969, when he went to the [[Institute for Defense Analyses]] in Washington, D.C., remaining there for two years and moving to [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]], in 1971 to work for [[Science Applications International Corporation]]. In 1974, he became a research physicist with the [[Institute for Pure and Applied Physical Sciences]] at the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref name="San Diego obit"/>

==Pioneering use of lasers in art conservation==
In 1971, Asmus met oceanographer [[Walter Munk]], who asked Asmus if he could make holograms of statues and art objects in Venice in order to preserve them.<ref name="Rauch">Mary S. Rauch, "The Newest in Science is Working To Save the Oldest in Art", ''Newport News Daily Press'' (December 28, 1980), ''Parade'' p. 16.</ref> Through this process, Asmus discerned that he could use lasers to remove detritus encrusting the statues without harming the underlying works.<ref name="Rauch"/> In 1972, Asmus "first applied laser cleaning to marble sculptures", and therefore "is considered to be the grandfather of laser art conservation".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.e-conservationline.com/content/view/720/239/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090522025736/http://www.e-conservationline.com/content/view/720/239/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=May 22, 2009 |title=LACONA VII Proceedings: Lasers in the Conservation of Artworks|first1=Rui|last1=Bordalo|publisher=eConservation Magazine|date=June 4, 2009}}</ref> That same year, Asmus worked with holography pioneer Ralph Wuerker, with whom he "proved the feasibility of creating full-size holograms of statuary, permitting three-dimensional reproductions of the world's sculptural masterpieces".<ref>"Laser Photography May Preserve Art", ''[[The Indianapolis Star]]'' (March 31, 1972), p. 36.</ref> Asmus continued working with Munk to create a three-dimensional record of the city of [[Venice]] in 1973, while continuing to investigate means of using lasers to clean statuary.<ref>"A Benevolent Beam", ''[[San Francisco Examiner]]'' (September 2, 1973), p. 30.</ref>

In 1975, Asmus developed "supersensitive sonar detectors" to assist art historian [[Carlo Pedretti]] and other scientists searching for ''[[The Battle of Anghiari (Leonardo)|The Battle of Anghiari]]'', a lost painting by [[Leonardo da Vinci]], at times referred to as "The Lost Leonardo", believed to be hidden beneath one of the later [[fresco]]es in the [[Palazzo Vecchio#Salone dei Cinquecento|Salone dei Cinquecento]] (Hall of the Five Hundred) in the [[Palazzo Vecchio]] in [[Florence]].<ref>Everett Holles, "Search For a Lost da Vinci", ''[[San Francisco Examiner]]'' (August 10, 1975), p. 19.</ref> In 1978, Asmus used laser technology to uncover artwork in the [[California State Capitol]] building that had been repeatedly painted over since a 1939 remodeling,<ref>"Laser finds Capitol art", ''The Berkeley Gazette'' (April 26, 1978), p. 26.</ref> ultimately removing nine layers of paint to restore the original artwork.<ref name="Rauch"/> In 1980, after vandals attempted to use an abrasive kitchen cleanser to deface ancient [[petroglyph]]s in [[Arches National Park]] in Utah, Asmus was called in to use his technology to repair the damage, and "succeeded in removing most of the cleanser".<ref name="Rauch"/>

His application of complex scientific devices to art enabled Asmus to work on many of the world's most famous cultural objects, including the ''[[Mona Lisa]]''.<ref>{{cite web|last1=de Leschery|first1=Karen|title=John Fredrich Asmus: Project|url=http://www.rolexawards.com/profiles/laureates/john_fredrich_asmus/project|website=Rolex Awards for Enterprise|language=en|date=2001}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1117/2.3201403.08| title = John Asmus: Optical techniques and the mysterious Mona Lisa| journal = SPIE Newsroom| year = 2014| last1 = Spie}}</ref> In the 1980s, Asmus "turned a personal fascination with the Mona Lisa into a five-year project to recapture the painting's original vitality".<ref name="Roth">Mark Roth, "Uncovering the Mona Lisa", ''[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]'' (March 2, 1987), p. 1.</ref> Pedretti had proposed that Leonardo had originally painted the ''Mona Lisa'' bare-breasted, and Asmus believed that he could determine whether this theory was correct, "using computer image enhancement techniques developed for interpreting satellite photographs".<ref name="Rauch"/> Asmus used [[computer image processing]] to examine images of the painting to determine how the colors would appear if they were not distorted by the yellowing of the aged varnish. By 1987, Asmus had discovered previously unknown evidence indicating that the subject had originally been painted with a necklace, which had apparently then been painted over by Leonardo.<ref name="Roth"/><ref name="Indiana Gazette">"Analysis of Mona Lisa turns up surprises", ''Indiana Gazette'' (May 20, 1996), p. 5.</ref><ref name="Standard Speaker">Kristine Moe, "Expert plans facelift for ancient Chinese artwork", ''Hazleton Standard-Speaker'' (December 8, 1987), p. 27.</ref> Asmus also determined that restorers had obscured mountains originally appearing in the background of the portrait, likely in order to emphasize foreground features.<ref name="Indiana Gazette"/>

In 1988, Asmus published his results from using this technology to compare the ''[[Isleworth Mona Lisa]]'' and the Louvre ''Mona Lisa'', finding that they shared a signature frequency of degrees of lightness and darkness, which Asmus concluded indicated that the examined aspects of both paintings were painted by the same person.<ref name="Asmus 1988">John F. Asmus, "Computer Studies of the Isleworth and Louvre Mona Lisas", in T. Russell Hsing and Andrew G. Tescher, ''Selected Papers on Visual Communication: Technology and Applications'' (SPIE Optical Engineering Press, 1990), p. 652-656; reprinted from ''Optical Engineering'', Vol. 28(7) (July 1989), p. 800-804.</ref> During this same period, Asmus also developed a plan to restore the Qin dynasty [[Terracotta Army]] in [[Xi'an]], China,<ref name="Standard Speaker"/> and to piece together a Renaissance fresco by [[Andrea Mantegna]] shattered by bombing in [[World War II]].<ref name="Standard Speaker"/> In 1990, he received a [[Rolex Awards for Enterprise|Rolex Enterprise Award]] for his conservation work on the terracotta warriors.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rolexawards.com/people|title=Rolex Awards for Enterprise|website=Rolex Awards for Enterprise : Profiles in A-F}}</ref>

In 2016 Asmus revisited the ''Isleworth Mona Lisa'' with professors [[Vadim Parfenov]] and [[Jessie Elford]], with the trio publishing the results of scientific examinations that established to their satisfaction that the same artist painted the face of both the ''Mona Lisa'' and the ''Isleworth Mona Lisa''.<ref name="Asmus Parfenov Elford">{{cite journal |last1=Asmus|first1=John F.|last2=Parfenov |first2=Vadim|last3=Elford|first3=Jessie|date= 28 November 2016 |title=Seeing double: Leonardo's Mona Lisa twin|journal= Optical and Quantum Electronics |volume=48|issue=12|pages=555 |doi=10.1007/s11082-016-0799-0|bibcode=2016OQEle..48..555A |s2cid=125226212}}</ref><ref name=Boudin>{{cite book |last=Boudin de l'Arche|first=Gerard|date=2017 |title=A la recherche de Monna Lisa |location=Cannes, France |publisher=Edition de l'Omnibus |isbn=9791095833017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.reuters.com/article/entertainment-us-art-monalisa-idUSBRE91C11H20130213 |title= New proof said found for "original" Mona Lisa – |publisher= Reuters.com |date= 13 February 2013 |accessdate= 26 July 2017}}</ref> In 2018, Asmus and Parfenov published findings on the application of the same technology to portraits by [[Rembrandt]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1296207418303716 |title=Characterization of Rembrandt self-portraits through digital-chiaroscuro statistics|first1=John F.|last1=Asmus|first2=Vadim|last2=Parfenov|journal=Journal of Cultural Heritage|date=December 28, 2018|volume=38 |pages=167–173 |doi=10.1016/j.culher.2018.12.005 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
In 1963, Asmus married Barbara Ann Flaherty, with whom he had two daughters. Barbara preceded him in death. Asmus died at his home in [[La Jolla, California]], on Easter Sunday, 2024, at the age of 87.<ref name="San Diego obit"/>
